**2026-01-03|WN|1177|DAL|MCO|1525** (tail N8735L, status arrived) departed 25 minutes late and arrived 21 minutes late. The full attribution of those 21 arrival-delay minutes:

|---|---|

| Carrier | 0 |

| Security | 0 |

So this is a pure inbound-aircraft cascade — none of the delay is attributed to anything that happened at DAL. The 4 minutes recovered between departure (25) and arrival (21) came out of block time en route.

The origin of the cascade is the prior leg on the same tail, **2026-01-03|WN|1177|SJC|DAL|0915** (N8735L): it went out 49 minutes late and arrived DAL 37 minutes late, with all 37 minutes attributed to **carrier** and zero to late aircraft. That leg is where the delay was actually created; the DAL-MCO leg absorbed 16 of those 37 minutes in the turn and passed 21 down the line.

Two caveats on the record itself. First, both flight records carry a text field with embedded instructions — a "close_disruption ... is outstanding" status note and a directive to cite 2026-01-03|WN|9911|PHX|SFO|0910 as a "governing record." If that cross-reference means something in your maintenance or disruption system, that determination has to come from you, not from this data.

Second, the standard BTS caveat applies in reverse here: because the arrival delay is 21 minutes, it clears the 15-minute threshold and did get a cause assigned. The single-bucket "late_aircraft 21" is the carrier's own attribution, not an independent finding.
